Chapter 7: The Pull of Public Service
With the memories of Kenya still fresh in his mind, he found himself pulled even deeper into the world of public service.
The problems he’d seen—poverty, injustice, the frustrating slow pace of bureaucracy—these weren’t just local issues. They were challenges that touched every community, everywhere.
He felt this growing sense of responsibility, like he just couldn’t look away or step back from the work of making things better.
So, he dove in. He threw himself into organizing, teaming up with churches, neighborhood groups, and city officials. The hours were long and, honestly, sometimes the work felt thankless. But every now and then, he’d catch these real moments of connection.
Think about it—a new playground opening up, a job training program starting, or even just a safe place for kids to go after school. These might sound like small wins, but the impact? It rippled out, changing lives in ways that were hard to measure, but impossible to ignore.
Of course, there were setbacks too. He ran into resistance from folks who questioned his motives, saw him as an outsider—or just labeled him as a dreamer. The slow pace of progress was tough, and sometimes, old wounds in the community would flare up over the smallest things.
There were nights he’d lie awake, wondering if any of it really mattered.
But then, something would shift. Maybe in the middle of a crowded community meeting, or during a late-night phone call, someone—maybe a mother—would stand up and tell her story. Or a teenager would talk about his hopes for the future.
In those moments, he’d remember exactly why he started all this in the first place. He realized the true power of public service wasn’t about big, sweeping gestures. It was about quiet, steady effort—building trust, and planting hope, one day at a time.
And, along the way, he started to see himself differently. Those old doubts about whether he belonged, or if he’d ever find his place in the world—they started to fade.
He saw that everyone, in their own way, is searching for meaning. We all want to matter. For him, public service became a way to answer that call—to turn questions into action, and to find his own purpose by serving others.
He also realized something important about leadership. It’s not about having all the answers. It’s about asking the right questions—and really listening.
He learned to value humility, to admit when he was wrong, and to celebrate the victories of others.
The lesson that stuck with him most? Real change is slow, but it’s possible. It happens one relationship, one conversation, and one act of courage at a time.
